subject: shapiro

brief.inclusion: Democratic governor of Pennsylvania since 2023 and former state attorney general, the most popular figure in the largest swing state, seeking reelection in November 2026 and widely seen as a 2028 presidential contender.
brief.namesakes: Many FEC contributors named Josh or Joshua Shapiro (Chappaqua, Wynnewood, Los Angeles, Wayne, Fairfax and others); his personal federal giving is negligible and is not matched. Distinct from commentator Ben Shapiro.

coverage.lags: Pennsylvania state campaign-finance records hold his campaign money. The November 3, 2026 result is pending.

summary: Democratic governor of Pennsylvania since January 2023, after six years as attorney general in which he released the 2018 grand-jury report finding 301 Catholic priests had abused more than 1,000 children. He beat Doug Mastriano by nearly 15 points in 2022, rebuilt a collapsed stretch of I-95 in 12 days, was a finalist to be Kamala Harris's running mate, and survived an April 2025 arson attack on the governor's residence hours after his family's Passover Seder. In October 2026 he led Republican Stacy Garrity 59–34 in a Quinnipiac poll.

works.title: Where We Keep the Light: Stories from a Life of Service

chapters.title: From Montgomery County to Harrisburg
chapters.dek: A Jewish day-school graduate, congressional aide and suburban officeholder.
chapters.body:
Shapiro was born on June 20, 1973, in Kansas City, Missouri, and grew up in Montgomery County, outside Philadelphia, in an observant Jewish household; he attended Akiba Hebrew Academy [[wikipedia]]. After graduating from the University of Rochester in 1995 he worked in Washington for members of Congress and at the Israeli embassy, then earned a Georgetown law degree in 2002 [[wikipedia, wikipedia-book]].

He won a seat in the Pennsylvania House in 2004 and served until 2012, then chaired the Montgomery County Board of Commissioners from 2012 to 2017 while practicing corporate law [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Attorney general
chapters.dek: The clergy-abuse report that made his national name.
chapters.body: Shapiro narrowly won the 2016 race for attorney general and was reelected in 2020 [[wikipedia]]. On August 14, 2018, he released a statewide grand-jury report, drawn from more than half a million pages of the dioceses' own records, identifying 301 priests in six Pennsylvania dioceses who had abused more than 1,000 children over seven decades. "It was child sexual abuse, including rape, committed by grown men, priests, against children," he said, rejecting church officials' descriptions of it as "horseplay and wrestling," and he told survivors, "we hear you, and we believe your truth" [[america-2018]]. In 2021 he helped secure about $1 billion for Pennsylvania from the national opioid settlement [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Governor of the biggest swing state
chapters.dek: A landslide over Mastriano and a 12-day highway rebuild.
chapters.body: Shapiro beat Republican Doug Mastriano by 56.5 to 41.7 percent in 2022, and was sworn in on January 17, 2023 [[wikipedia]]. When a tanker fire collapsed an elevated section of I-95 in Philadelphia that June, the state reopened six lanes 12 days later, far ahead of early estimates; "Let this serve as an example to all that Pennsylvania can do big things," he said [[pa-i95-2023]]. He dropped four-year degree requirements for most state jobs [[wikipedia]]. During the 2024 Penn encampment he called for police to clear protesters [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Running mate finalist, arson target, 2028 prospect
chapters.dek: A national profile built across two years.
chapters.body:
After Joe Biden withdrew in July 2024, Shapiro endorsed Kamala Harris and was one of three finalists she interviewed on August 4 for running mate; she chose Tim Walz [[wikipedia]]. In his January 2026 memoir, Where We Keep the Light, he wrote that her vetting team had asked whether he had ever been an agent of the Israeli government, a question he called offensive; Harris's team said such questions were standard [[wikipedia-book, wikipedia]].

In the early hours of April 13, 2025, hours after the Shapiros hosted a Passover Seder at the governor's residence, Cody Balmer scaled the fence and set the house on fire with homemade incendiary devices. State troopers evacuated the family and no one was hurt [[spotlight-arson-2025]]. Shapiro said that "if he was trying to terrorize our family, our friends, the Jewish community," no one would deter them from celebrating their faith [[spotlight-arson-2025]]. Balmer pleaded guilty to attempted murder and terrorism in October 2025 and was sentenced to 25 to 50 years [[ap-balmer-2025]].

Shapiro announced in January 2026 that he would seek a second term [[wikipedia]]. An October Quinnipiac poll found him leading Republican Stacy Garrity 59 to 34 percent with 63 percent approval [[quinnipiac-2026]]. He is widely discussed as a 2028 presidential candidate [[wikipedia-book]].
